content: Niacin, also known as nicotinic acid or 3-pyridinecarboxylic acid, is a white, crystalline powder that is highly soluble in water. Its structural formula is well-defined. NIASPAN is an oral, film-coated, medium-orange tablet that is available in three strengths: 500 mg, 750 mg, and 1000 mg of niacin. These tablets also contain inactive ingredients such as hypromellose, povidone, stearic acid, and polyethylene glycol, along with coloring agents like FD&C Yellow 6/Sunset Yellow FCF Aluminum Lake, synthetic red and yellow iron oxides, and titanium dioxide. Pharmacodynamics Niacin is metabolized in the body to form nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) within the NAD coenzyme system. Unlike nicotinamide, niacin in gram doses reduces total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and triglycerides (TG), while increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). The extent of these effects can vary depending on the severity and type of underlying lipid abnormalities. The increase in HDL-C is associated with a rise in apolipoprotein A-I (Apo A-I) levels and a redistribution of HDL subfractions, including an increased HDL2:HDL3 ratio and elevated levels of lipoprotein A-I (Lp A-I), an HDL-C particle containing only Apo A-I. Niacin therapy also lowers serum levels of apolipoprotein B-100 (Apo B), the primary protein component of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and LDL fractions, as well as Lp(a), a variant form of LDL linked to coronary risk. Preliminary evidence suggests that niacin may favorably alter LDL particle size, though the clinical significance of this effect remains uncertain. The impact of niacin-induced lipid and protein changes on cardiovascular morbidity or mortality in individuals without preexisting coronary artery disease has not been established. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated that elevated levels of TC, LDL-C, and Apo B contribute to human atherosclerosis. Conversely, reduced HDL-C levels are associated with the development of atherosclerosis. Epidemiological research has shown that cardiovascular morbidity and mortality are directly proportional to TC and LDL-C levels and inversely proportional to HDL-C levels. Cholesterol-enriched, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, such as VLDL, intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), and their remnants, can also promote atherosclerosis. Elevated plasma TG levels are often found in conjunction with low HDL-C levels and small LDL particles, as well as with non-lipid metabolic risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD). However, total plasma TG has not consistently been shown to be an independent risk factor for CHD. Additionally, the independent effects of raising HDL-C or lowering TG on coronary and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality risk remain undetermined. Pharmacokinetics Absorption Niacin undergoes extensive and saturable first-pass metabolism, resulting in dose-dependent and highly variable concentrations in systemic circulation. Following NIASPAN administration, the time to reach maximum plasma niacin concentrations is approximately 5 hours. To minimize the risk of gastrointestinal (GI) upset, it is recommended to take NIASPAN with a low-fat meal or snack. Single-dose bioavailability studies have shown that the 500 mg and 1000 mg tablet strengths are dosage form equivalent, but the 500 mg and 750 mg strengths are not. Metabolism Niacin's pharmacokinetics are complex due to extensive first-pass metabolism, which is dose-rate specific and saturable at the doses used to treat dyslipidemia. In humans, one metabolic pathway involves conjugation with glycine to form nicotinuric acid (NUA), which is excreted in the urine. There may be limited reversible metabolism back to niacin. Another pathway leads to the formation of NAD, though it is unclear whether nicotinamide is a precursor to or a product of NAD synthesis. Nicotinamide is further metabolized to N-methylnicotinamide (MNA) and nicotinamide-N-oxide (NNO). MNA is subsequently metabolized to N-methyl-2-pyridone-5-carboxamide (2PY) and N-methyl-4-pyridone-5-carboxamide (4PY), with 2PY being the predominant metabolite in humans. At therapeutic doses for hyperlipidemia, these metabolic pathways become saturable, explaining the nonlinear relationship between niacin dose and plasma concentrations following multiple-dose NIASPAN administration. Nicotinamide does not exhibit hypolipidemic activity, and the activity of other metabolites is unknown. Elimination After single and multiple doses, approximately 60-76% of the niacin dose administered as NIASPAN is recovered in the urine as niacin and its metabolites. Up to 12% is excreted as unchanged niacin after multiple dosing. The ratio of metabolites recovered in the urine depends on the administered dose. Special Populations Pediatric Use: No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in individuals aged 16 years or younger. Geriatric Use: No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in individuals older than 65 years. Renal Impairment: No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in patients with renal impairment. NIASPAN should be used cautiously in patients with renal disease. Hepatic Impairment: No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in patients with hepatic impairment. Active liver disease, unexplained transaminase elevations, and significant or unexplained hepatic dysfunction are contraindications to NIASPAN use.
